newsitem.title: ROMANIA: Romania hopes Chirac visit will be NATO ticket. [CORRECTED 15:33 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Romania hopes Chirac visit will be NATO ticket. [CORRECTED 15:33 GMT]

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac started the first visit to Bucharest in six years by a major Western leader on Friday, with Romania's new centrist government hoping he can help get their country into NATO.

Officials planned a lavish welcome for Chirac, the most vocal advocate of Romania's outsider bid for inclusion in NATO's first wave of expansion. The alliance will announce who will be invited to join in July, despite bitter opposition from Russia.
Chirac was met by President Emil Constantinescu and a 21-gun salute at Otopeni airport, state radio said in a live broadcast.
Thousands of well-wishers gathered hours ahead of Chirac's arrival for his official welcome at the Arch of Triumph, Bucharest's slightly smaller version of the Paris monument.
Chirac, on a two-day state visit, was then to be driven to the presidential Cotroceni palace down boulevards decked out in Romanian and French tricolour flags.
"The fact that France provides our most solid support among NATO member states is already well known," Constantinescu told a radio interviewer on Friday before Chirac's arrival.
"President Chirac has repeatedly conveyed...the message of France's strong support. The position is very clear."
Romania was not a favoured port of call for Western leaders under Constantinescu's ex-communist predecessor Ion Iliescu.

Chirac is the first to visit since 1991, when the man he succeeded, the late Francois Mitterrand, was also given a lavish reception. France has long-standing cultural and other ties with Romania, Eastern Europe's only Latin nation.

Although Hungary, Poland and the Czech Republic are the favourites for NATO expansion eastwards, Constantinescu's defeat of Iliescu and pledges by the new centrist government to speed market reforms appear to have improved Romania's prospects. Slovenia is also seen as an outsider with a chance.
"We can still catch the train to NATO," the daily Adevarul said in a front-page editorial.

Romania argues that its position on the Black Sea and proximity to Poland and ex-Soviet Ukraine make its inclusion a strategic trump card for NATO and hopes Chirac can persuade Washington to back its rapid admission.
But U.S. officials accompanying Secretary of State Madeleine Albright on a European tour this week said Romania was still an unlikely prospect -- a view shared by many other allies.

In Moscow, Albright said after talks with President Boris Yeltsin that "very important progress" had been made in trying to reassure Russia's that NATO enlargement poses no threat. But she added that complex issues still had to be resolved.

On the eve of his two-day visit, Chirac said Russia was linking the admission of up to five new members to a formal agreement with NATO. He said Yeltsin had made no objections to Romanian membership during talks in Moscow earlier this month.
During recent visits to Poland and Hungary, Chirac backed their bid for European Union membership by the year 2000.

French officials said Chirac was likely to be more vague in his pledges towards Romania with regard to the EU, since it has lagged far behind those ex-communist states in its reform drive since the execution of dictator Nicolae Ceausescu in 1989.
Chirac's visit includes an address to parliament's two chambers later on Friday and a question-and-answer session on Saturday with Bucharest University students.
(Corrects Chirac's schedule)

One difficult issue on the visit is the periodic deportations by chartered aircraft of Romanian nationals found to have entered France illegally. During Chirac's stay, the two countries' interior ministers were due to sign an accord on crime and illegal migration.
